newsitem.title: zaire: MORE ZAIRE FIGHTING REPORTED, U.N. SEEKS REFUGEES.
newsitem.headline: MORE ZAIRE FIGHTING REPORTED, U.N. SEEKS REFUGEES.

text.p: Renewed fighting was reported in eastern Zaire on Thursday as rebels, backed by Rwanda, hunted down Hutu gunmen while U.N. agencies stepped up the hunt for some 700,000 missing refugees.
"We are receiving first-hand reports of fighting around Minove and in the Masisi hills above Sake," Filippo Grandi, head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR told reporters in Goma.
He said that after almost a day of wrangling the UNHCR had finally succeeded in obtaining access to Sake where several thousands of refugees were believed to have gathered.
"We have been able to gain access to Sake and things there do not appear to be as bad as we had thought," he added.

Refugees arriving in Goma from Sake told reporters there had been several clashes in the last few days between the rebels and members of the ex-Rwandan army and Interahamwe militia, blamed for leading the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

Access for reporters outside the town of Goma, through which an estimated half a million Hutu refugees poured back into Rwanda last week, was blocked and repeated attempts to contact rebel commanders were unsuccessful.

U.N. agencies, dismissing statements by Rwanda that the vast majority of refugees had now returned home, have stepped up a search for an estimated 700,000 refugees still believed to be scattered across eastern Zaire.
The U.N. said it had succeeded in sending an assessment team into Bukavu. Zairean rebels have up until now prevented aid agencies from entering Bukavu to gain a first-hand picture.
Some 200,000 refugees, many of whom fled fighting into the bush, are still believed to be in that area and a further 500,000 further south near Bukavu, south of Lake Kivu.
"We are absolutely desperate to locate these 700,000," Peter Kessler, UNHCR spokesman in Nairobi, told Reuters.
He said the assessment team had been told by the Zairean rebels that all camps in the area were now empty and the refugees had fled several hundred km (miles) westwards and southwards.
"But I stress, there is no independent confirmation of that, that is why we need people in there," he said.

Rwanda, always reluctant to see a U.N. multinational force in the region, maintains nearly all the refugees returned in last week's human wave, a fact which -- if true -- could have a crucial impact on plans to send a U.N. force.
Major-General Paul Kagame, vice-president and defence minister of Rwanda, said in Kigali on Wednesday he believed the numbers of refugees in camps in Zaire had been exaggerated.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda after the 1994 massacre of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

They returned en masse to escape a new war in which Zairean rebels broke the hold of soldiers from the remnants of Rwanda's defeated army and the militias over fellow refugees who claim they were prevented from returning home earlier.

Meanwhile, Canada, the country set to lead any multinational intervention, said on Thursday military leaders from countries expected to send troops would finally meet on Friday in Germany. The meeting was originally scheduled for Wednesday.
"In general terms, the meeting will be held to determine and decide on the general scope of the mission," Canadian Navy Reserve Lieutenant Charles Brown told Reuters.

Military leaders from several nations including the United States, France, Britain and Canada were expected to attend the meeting, which was called to review plans for the mission endorsed by the U.N. before last week's mass return.

Canada said most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid to refugees and displaced Zaireans scattered through the war-torn Great Lakes region.
Emma Bonino, the European Union's humanitarian aid Commissioner, accused the world community on Thursday of indifference bordering on racism over the plight of the stranded refugees.

"How many lives have to be in danger, how many people missing to justify a deployment of troops by the civilised world'? Who sets the threshold -- is it 500,000, 200,000, 100,000 or 10,000?" she said at the European Parliament.
"Is it the colour of their skin which makes the difference, which leads us to believe that it is their inevitable lot to be linked to a cycle of...massacres?"

Bonino said a proposed U.N. multinational force was essential to allow humanitarian aid workers to save lives in Zaire. Without that protection, aid workers risked being killed and taken hostage, she said.
